Today is the twentieth of Rajab in the year one thousand four hundred and fifteen (AH). It has been our custom to begin this session with the exegesis (tafsir) of verses from the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because the Book of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, was revealed for several wise purposes:

Among them: worship of Allah, the Exalted, through its recitation, for reciting the Book of Allah brings one closer to Allah, and for each letter of it there is a reward of ten good deeds.

It was also revealed for the sake of reflecting upon its meanings, as He, the Exalted, says: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad 29]. This wisdom has been neglected by many people. I do not say ordinary people; even among students of knowledge you find some students who take care to explain the hadiths, or the words of the jurists, or others among the scholars of the Sharia, but they do not take care with the tafsir of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, even though the Book of Allah is the mother of all books and all books refer back to it. The Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is what we have been charged to reflect upon its verses and to take admonition from. Therefore, we see that it is not befitting for a student of knowledge to turn away from the tafsir of the Book of Allah while he is occupied with the tafsir of the words of other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

We began this tafsir with Surat an-Naba', because this portion is often recited in the prayers, such as the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers, and the common people hear it, so it is good that they know the meanings of this portion of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

The verses of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in the Glorious Book are similar to one another. You may find some verses identical in wording in another place, such as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh upon them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [at-Tawbah 73, at-Tahrim 9]. Today's session, the one in which we will speak about from the Book of Allah, is Surat (Iqra') (Read); since, praise be to Allah, we have completed what preceded it.

Whoever wishes to return to it, let him return.

And it has been said: seeking help through that; that is, read seeking help through the name of Allah, because all of Allah's names are good and all are aid, which a person seeks help through. For this reason a person seeks help through them for his ablution, seeks help through them for his eating, and seeks help through them for his intercourse; they are all a help.

For this reason He said ﴿created﴾ and omitted the object, indicating generality, because omitting the object conveys generality; if the object had been mentioned, the act would be restricted to it. Do you understand this statement? That is, if He had said "created such-and-such," the creating would have been restricted to what was mentioned only; but when He says "created" without restriction, it becomes general. He is the Creator of everything, exalted is He.

Then He said: ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾, specifying and singling out the creation of man, as an honour and dignity for man, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam and carried them on the land and sea and provided for them of the good things and preferred them over much of what We have created, with decided preference﴾ [al-Isra' 70]. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has made clear that He created man from 'alaq, but it develops. This is the beginning of creation connected with Adam.

The other creation, of his descendants, begins with a drop (nutfah), which is base water and gushing water. This drop remains in the womb for forty days, then it changes little by little. When forty days are complete, it transforms by development and gradual progression until it becomes blood, an 'alaqah. Then it begins to grow and thicken and develop little by little. When eighty days are complete, it passes into a lump (mudghah), a piece of flesh the size of what a person chews, and it remains so for forty days. So this is one hundred and twenty days, and in months how many? Four months. After four months, Allah sends to it the angel appointed over the wombs, who breathes the soul into it, and the soul enters the body by the permission of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. We cannot know the reality, essence, and substance of the soul; we do not know of what substance it is. We know the body: where it came from? Its origin is from earth, then in the wombs of women from the drop. But the soul, we do not know of what essence or substance it is: ﴿And they ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is of the affair of my Lord, and you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [al-Isra' 85]. The angel breathes the soul into this fetus, and it begins to move, because its first growth was like the growth of trees without sensation. After the soul is breathed into it, it becomes a human being who moves. For this reason, if a miscarriage occurs before four months, it is buried in any place on the earth without washing, shrouding, or funeral prayer over it, and it is not resurrected because it is not yet a human being. After four months, if it is miscarried, it must be washed, shrouded, prayed over, and buried in the graveyards, because it has become a human being. It is also named, because on the Day of Resurrection it will be called by its name, and an 'aqiqah is performed for it, though the 'aqiqah for it is not as emphasized as the 'aqiqah for one who has reached seven days after birth.

In any case, this fetus in its mother's womb develops until it becomes a human being. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, permits its emergence into the world after a period that is usually at most nine months.

On this occasion I would like to make clear that man has four abodes: the first abode is in his mother's womb, the second is in this world, the third is in the barzakh, and the fourth is in Paradise or Hell, which is the final destination.

﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾: what did we say about 'alaq? It is the collective noun of 'alaqah, which is a well-known worm-like form of blood, and this is the first origin of man, from which the material of life, which is blood, is formed.

﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous (3). Who taught by the pen (4). Taught man that which he knew not﴾ [al-'Alaq 3-5].

﴿Read﴾ is a repetition of the first. But is it emphasis (tawkid) or establishment (ta'sis)?

The correct view is that it is establishment (ta'sis). The first ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ was joined with what relates to lordship, and ﴿and your Lord is the Most Generous (3). Who taught by the pen﴾ with what relates to the Sharia. The first relates to destiny (qadar), and the second to the Sharia, because teaching by the pen is what the Sharia most depends upon, since the Sharia is written and preserved: the Quran is written and preserved, the Sunnah is written and preserved, and the words of the scholars are written and preserved. For this reason Allah repeated it a second time. Allah willing, the rest of the discussion of this verse will come, because (...).

Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgement.

To proceed: this is the eighty-second session of the lecture series known as "the open door" session, which takes place every Thursday of the week. Today is the twentieth of Rajab in the year one thousand four hundred and fifteen (AH). It has been our custom to begin this session with the exegesis (tafsir) of verses from the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because the Book of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, was revealed for several wise purposes:

Among them: worship of Allah, the Exalted, through its recitation, for reciting the Book of Allah brings one closer to Allah, and for each letter of it there is a reward of ten good deeds.

It was also revealed for the sake of reflecting upon its meanings, as He, the Exalted, says: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may reflect upon its verses and that people of understanding may be reminded﴾ [Sad 29]. This wisdom has been neglected by many people. I do not say ordinary people; even among students of knowledge you find some students who take care to explain the hadiths, or the words of the jurists, or others among the scholars of the Sharia, but they do not take care with the tafsir of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, even though the Book of Allah is the mother of all books and all books refer back to it. The Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is what we have been charged to reflect upon its verses and to take admonition from. Therefore, we see that it is not befitting for a student of knowledge to turn away from the tafsir of the Book of Allah while he is occupied with the tafsir of the words of other than Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

We began this tafsir with Surat an-Naba', because this portion is often recited in the prayers, such as the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers, and the common people hear it, so it is good that they know the meanings of this portion of the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

The verses of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, in the Glorious Book are similar to one another. You may find some verses identical in wording in another place, such as His saying: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh upon them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [at-Tawbah 73, at-Tahrim 9]. This verse appears with the same wording in another place in the Book of Allah: it appears in at-Tawbah and it appears in Surat at-Tahrim. Thus the Book of Allah resembles its parts one another.

Today's session, the one in which we will speak about from the Book of Allah, is Surat (Iqra') (Read); since, praise be to Allah, we have completed what preceded it.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Bestower of Mercy. ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq 1].

God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Nay! Verily, man does transgress, because he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq 6–7].

﴿كَلَّا﴾ (kallā) in the Noble Qur'an has several meanings. Among them, it may mean "truly" (haqqan), as in this verse. So ﴿كَلَّا﴾ means "truly." That is, God affirms this with an affirmation free of any doubt.

﴿Verily, man does transgress, because he sees himself self-sufficient﴾. ﴿الْإِنْسَانَ﴾ (al-insān, "man") is not a specific individual; rather, it refers to the species: every human being from the children of Adam who sees himself as self-sufficient will transgress. Transgression (ṭughyān) is going beyond the limit. When he sees that he is independent of God's mercy, he transgresses and does not care. When he sees that he is independent of God, the Mighty and Majestic, in relieving distress and obtaining what he seeks, he no longer turns to God or cares for Him. When he sees that he is independent through health, he forgets sickness; when he sees that he is independent through being full, he forgets hunger; when he sees that he is independent through clothing, he forgets nakedness... and so on. Thus man, by his nature, is inclined to transgression and rebellion whenever he sees himself in wealth. But the believer is excluded from this, because the believer does not see himself as independent of God for the blink of an eye. He is always in need of God, the Glorified and Exalted. He asks his Lord for every need, and seeks refuge in Him at every hardship. He knows that if God leaves him to himself, He leaves him to weakness, helplessness, and vulnerability, and that he possesses for himself no benefit or harm. This is the believer. But man, insofar as he is man, is by nature inclined to transgression. This is like the saying of God, the Exalted: ﴿And man bore it; verily, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72].

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said, threatening this tyrant: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ [Al-Alaq 8]. That is, the return (al-maraji'). Meaning: however much you transgress, exalt yourself, act arrogantly, and consider yourself self-sufficient, your return is to Allah, mighty and majestic. As Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿Except for one who turns away and disbelieves. Then Allah will punish him with the greatest punishment. Indeed, to Us is their return. Then indeed, upon Us is their account﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 23-26]. And if the return is to Allah in all matters, then no one can ever escape the decree of Allah, nor His reward and justice.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾, we may say that it is more general than the warning and threat. That is, it includes the warning and threat, but it may also include something more general, so the meaning would be that the return to Allah is in everything. In legislative matters, to what is judgment referred? To the Book and the Sunnah: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa 59]. And in universal matters, to whom is the reference? To Allah: ﴿When you sought help from your Lord, and He answered you﴾ [Al-Anfal 9]. So there is no return for the servant except to Allah. Then He said: ﴿Nay! If he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq 15]. ﴿Kallā﴾ here means "truly" (ḥaqqan). It may also be for deterrence (radʻ), meaning: to deter him from his evil act which he used to commit against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Or it means: truly, We will surely seize him by the forelock.

The clause ﴿la-nasfaʻan﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, the implied meaning being: "By Allah, if he does not desist, We will surely seize him by the forelock." The answer to the conditional was omitted and the answer to the oath remained, because this is the rule in the Arabic language: when an oath and a conditional come together, the answer of the one that comes later is omitted. Ibn Mālik said in his Alfiyya:

"Omit, when a conditional and an oath come together, the answer of whichever comes last, for it is what is required."

Here, the one that comes later is the conditional ﴿la-in﴾, and the oath is implied before it, since its implied meaning is: "By Allah, if he does not desist, We will surely seize him."

The meaning of ﴿la-nasfaʻan﴾ is: "We will surely seize him forcefully." The "forelock" (al-nāṣiyah) is the front part of the head, and the definite article in it, i.e., in "al-nāṣiyah," is the article of prior reference (al-ʻahd). Which reference is it? The mental reference (al-ʻahd al-dhihnī). The intended forelock here is the forelock of Abū Jahl, who threatened the Prophet (ﷺ) over his prayer and forbade him from it; i.e., "We will surely seize him by his forelock."

Is the intended meaning seizing by the forelock in this world, or that he will be dragged by his forelock into the Fire in the Hereafter?

This may be either. It may be that he is seized by the forelock, and he was indeed seized by the forelock on the day of Badr when he was killed along with those of the polytheists who were killed. And it may be that he is seized by the forelock on the Day of Resurrection and cast into the Fire, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks, and they will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾ [al-Raḥmān 41]. When a verse is suitable for two meanings that do not contradict one another, the obligation is to take it according to both meanings together, as is well known, and as we established previously and affirm now: when a verse may bear two meanings neither of which negates the other, the obligation is to take both meanings together.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 96, verse 16:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq 16]. ﴿A forelock﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the first "forelock," and it is a substitution of an indefinite noun for a definite one, which is permissible in the Arabic language. He said ﴿a forelock﴾ in order to make way for the description that follows it, which is His saying: ﴿lying, sinful﴾.

﴿Lying﴾ means that it is described as being characterized by lying. And there is no doubt that among the greatest forms of lying is what is uttered by the disbelievers who claim that there are other gods besides Allah. Indeed, this is the most lying of speech and the most evil of deeds.

﴿Sinful﴾ means: one who commits sin deliberately. And let it be known that there is a difference between (khati') and (mukhti'). The khati' is one who commits a sin deliberately, while the mukhti' is one who commits it out of ignorance. The latter is excused, and the former is not excused. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿None eats it except the sinners [al-khati'un]﴾ [al-Haqqah 37], meaning those who commit sin deliberately. And He, exalted, said: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err [akhta'na]﴾ [al-Baqarah 286], and Allah said: "I have done so" [[Recorded by Muslim (126/200) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. Similar to this is (qasit) and (muqsit): the qasit is the unjust, and the muqsit is the just. Allah said: ﴿And act justly; indeed, Allah loves those who act justly [al-muqsitin]﴾ [al-Hujurat 9], and He said: ﴿As for the unjust [al-qasitun], they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn 15]. So ﴿sinful﴾ means: one who deliberately commits wrongdoing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 96, verses 17–18:

﴿Then let him call upon his council (of men).﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 17, 18] The lam here is for challenge; meaning: if he is truthful and has strength and power, then let him call upon his council.

Al-nadi (the council) is the gathering place of a people for conversing among themselves, speaking together, and finding companionship with one another. Abu Jahl was held in high regard among the Quraysh, and he had a council to which people gathered and in which they spoke about their affairs. So here Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: if he is truthful, then let him call upon his council. There is no doubt that this is a challenge, just as you say to your enemy: if you have people, then come forward, and similar words that indicate challenge.

He said: ﴿We will call the guards of Hell.﴾ Meaning: we have with us those who are greater than this man's council, namely the Zabaniyah, the angels of the Fire; we ask Allah for well-being.

Allah the Exalted has described the angels of the Fire as ﴿harsh and severe﴾: harsh in disposition and severe in strength. ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded﴾ [At-Tahrim: 6]; they do not fail to carry out all that Allah commands them. Thus He described them with two attributes: that they are in complete submission to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾, and that they have complete ability, ﴿and do what they are commanded﴾.

Failure to carry out the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is either due to incapacity or due to disobedience. For example, one who does not pray the obligatory prayer while standing may do so out of incapacity, or out of stubbornness; he does not carry out the command of Allah. But the angels who are over the Fire have no incapacity; they have strength and power, and they have no arrogance toward the command, but rather complete humility and submission. These Zabaniyah, it is impossible for this man, his people, and his council to confront them ever. Therefore He said: ﴿We will call the guards of Hell.﴾

If someone says: where is the waw in His saying ﴿sanad'u﴾?

We say: it is elided because of the meeting of two sukun (quiescent letters); since the waw is sakin and the hamzah (hamzat al-wasl) is sakin too. When two sakin letters meet, if the first letter is sahih (a consonant), it is given kasra; and if it is not sahih (a weak letter), it is elided. Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in al-Kafiyah:

When two quiescent letters meet, vowel the first with kasra that precedes;
And if it is a soft letter, its deletion is due.

Meaning: when two sakin letters meet, if the first letter is sahih and not one of the letters of weakness (ʿillah), it takes kasra; like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved did not (cease)﴾ [Al-Bayyinah: 1], and its original form is (lam yakunu), because lam, when it enters a verb, jazms it, as in His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [Al-Ikhlas: 4]. But here two sakin letters met and the first was a sahih letter, so it took kasra.

As for when the first is a letter of softness (harf layn), meaning a letter of weakness, it is elided, as in this verse: ﴿sanad'u al-Zabaniyah﴾.
